cards.title: What the Choosing a Local Model guide is
questions: what is tayler's guide to picking an open model
guide to choosing local llms by tayler erbe
what is the choosing a local model guide
what is the practical guide to choosing a local model
what does tayler's local model guide cover
why did you write the choosing a local model guide
what is the find evaluate validate fine-tune guide
explain the local model selection guide on the portfolio
what is in the open-weight model selection guide
summarize the choosing a local model guide
what problem does the local model guide solve
how is the local model guide structured
when was the choosing a local model guide published
what is the october 2026 advisory guide
tell me about the model selection advisory guide
what sections are in the choosing a local model guide
cards.answer: It's an advisory guide from October 2026 for teams choosing an open-weight model for a specific job. Model names are full of numbers like 8B, 27B, 35B-A3B, Q4 and AWQ that look like a ranking and aren't one, so the guide explains what the labels mean, how models are commonly trained, why a smaller model can beat a bigger one on a task, and a method for picking, validating and, only when needed, fine-tuning. It combines findings from my own generation screen and document intelligence evaluation with general engineering guidance. It was independently reviewed and revised after technical feedback.

cards.title: How to read a model name like 27B or Q4
questions: how do you read a model name in the local model guide
what do 27b and 32b mean in a model name
what does the b in 32b stand for
does a bigger parameter count mean a better model
what do model name numbers tell you according to the guide
what does parameter count not tell you about a model
does 27b versus 32b rank the models
what does the choosing a local model guide say about reading model names
are 8b 27b 32b a ranking
what does the version or release date of a model tell you
does model size or release date identify the best model for a task
cards.answer: Those numbers are not a ranking. 27B or 32B means roughly that many billion parameters, the numbers the model learned in training. It's a design choice that sets capacity, but it says nothing about how well the model was trained or how well it follows instructions. Version and release date identify a release, and its documentation may disclose training changes and data, yet neither size nor release date alone identifies the best model for a task. That's the first lesson of the guide: treat the label as a starting point and test the model on your own job.

cards.title: Mixture of experts and active parameters in the guide
questions: what does 35b-a3b mean in the local model guide
what is a mixture of experts model according to the guide
what do active parameters mean for a mixture of experts model
is active parameter count a quality score
do mixture of experts models need less memory
why is a 3b active model not the same as a 3b dense model
does sparse activation make a model faster
what does a35b-a3b tell you about speed and storage
moe total parameters versus active parameters per token
how does the guide treat mixture of experts models
cards.answer: 35B-A3B names a mixture of experts: roughly 35 billion parameters in total, about 3 billion active per token, depending on the vendor's counting convention. Sparse activation can reduce computation compared with a similar dense model, but actual speed depends on the hardware and the serving software, and all the weights still need storing, so memory isn't saved. Active parameter count is also not a quality score. In the guide I treat it as one fact about cost and capacity, to be confirmed by measuring the model on my own hardware and task.

cards.title: Quantisation formats Q4 and AWQ in the guide
questions: what do q4 and q4_k_m mean in the local model guide
is awq a bit width or a method
what does the guide say about quantisation
does quantization shrink the context cache
why can the same model behave differently under different quantisation methods
how do you check the bit width of an awq checkpoint
what does q4 quantisation not shrink
does 4-bit quantisation change model behavior in the guide
what should I verify about a quantised checkpoint before downloading it
why does quantisation method matter when comparing local models
cards.answer: Q4 and Q4_K_M are approximately 4-bit weight formats with some mixed precision and storage overhead. They shrink the weights so a large model fits on one card, but not every other use of memory, such as the context cache. AWQ is a quantisation method, not a bit width, so check the actual bit width of the checkpoint you download. Different methods lose different things, so the same model can behave differently under each. That's why the guide says to run the same model under each quantisation you're considering instead of assuming they match.

cards.title: Instruct, base and thinking models in the guide
questions: what is the difference between instruct and base models in the local model guide
when should I use a base model instead of an instruct model
what do thinking or reasoning models do according to the guide
does reasoning mode cost time and token budget
can you turn off the reasoning of a thinking model
which variant is the usual starting point for an assistant application
what does chat or instruct mean in a model name
how does the guide describe thinking and reasoning variants
what do base models suit according to the guide
cards.answer: Instruct and chat models are adapted to respond to requests, and they're usually the starting point for assistant-style applications. Base models are mainly pretrained continuation models and suit specialized adaptation. Thinking or reasoning models may generate intermediate reasoning tokens before the final answer. That can help hard problems, but whether you can see or switch off the reasoning depends on the model and the server, and it costs time and token budget. In the guide I list reasoning mode among the settings to record, because it changes both results and cost.

cards.title: How open-weight models are commonly trained in the guide
questions: how does a model go from pretraining to an assistant in the guide
pretraining to assistant stages in the local model guide
how are open-weight models commonly trained according to the local model guide
what are the three stages of training in the guide
what is pretraining versus instruction tuning versus preference optimisation
what does supervised instruction tuning do
how does preference optimization or reinforcement learning shape a model
why do size and release date only start the comparison of models
what does the guide say about next-token prediction at scale
where does a model's knowledge and fluency come from
where do the preferences come from in model post-training
is the three-stage recipe universal for every model
cards.answer: The guide describes a common recipe in three stages, and says plainly it's not universal because vendors publish different amounts of detail. Pretraining is next-token prediction over very large amounts of text and code, often trillions of tokens, and it gives much of the knowledge and fluency. Supervised instruction tuning trains on requests paired with good responses, which turns a continuation model into an assistant. Preference optimization or reinforcement learning then pushes toward preferred responses, whether the preferences come from people, a reward model or automatic checks. Data, compute and all three stages matter alongside parameter count.

cards.title: Qwen3.8 27B versus Qwen3-32B in the generation screen
questions: how did qwen3.8 27b compare with qwen3-32b in the generation screen
how many groups did qwen3.8 27b accept in the local model guide
what was the replication result for qwen3.8 27b
what is the 21.7 point difference with a 95% interval of 6.6 to 35.5
did the smaller qwen model outperform qwen3-32b
what did the second pre-registered round on 60 new groups show
24 accepted against 11 for qwen3.8 27b
7 of 20 test groups accepted by qwen3.8 27b versus 3
what screening rule did qwen3.8 27b meet
is qwen3.8 27b adopted to replace qwen3-32b
cards.answer: In my generation screen, Qwen3.8 27B accepted 7 of 20 test groups through a strict generator's checks, against 3 for the larger Qwen3-32B configuration it would replace, which met a pre-registered screening rule. A second pre-registered round on 60 new groups replicated it: 24 accepted against 11, a difference of 21.7 points with a 95% interval of 6.6 to 35.5. It's still a comparison of configurations, one on Ollama and one on vLLM, on one job's groups, and adopting it remains a release decision.

cards.title: The prompt conflict found in the generation screen
questions: can i trust the qwen3.8 numbers given the flawed prompt in the guide
what prompt conflict did the local model guide find
why does the each other conflict matter for the generation screen results
was the prompt in the screen clean
what does pinned prompt checked by hash mean in the generation screen
can the screen figures be read as general instruction-following of qwen
what must happen before adopting a model after a prompt conflict
how did the review of the generation screen prompt change the claim
what is wrong with the prompt used in the qwen3.8 screen
cards.answer: A prompt review found that one rule banned the phrase "each other" while another required wording containing it. Every arm in the screen ran the same pinned prompt, the one with the conflict, copied from the release version and checked by hash. So the figures are pipeline outcomes under that prompt, not a clean measure of either model's general instruction-following. A corrected prompt has to be versioned and re-tested on both models before any adoption. I kept the finding in the guide because it limits what the numbers can claim.

cards.title: Checker flags at the first plan in the generation screen
questions: what were the plan check flags for qwen3.8 27b versus qwen3-32b
how many groups did the copying check flag for the smaller model
what is the causal-leap check in the generation screen
what is the behaviour-only check flagged 9 against 0
how many groups failed the exact-anchor check
why did the smaller model trade one failure for another
are the first plan checker flags counts across retries
do the plan flags amount to a semantic audit
what does a new model trade in the local model guide
what were the flagged counts 2 against 7 and 0 against 4
cards.answer: At the first plan check, the smaller model's plans were flagged by the copying check in 2 groups against 7 and by the causal-leap check in 0 against 4. But the behaviour-only check, which also covers feelings, causes, outcomes and labels, flagged 9 against 0. Both models were flagged by the exact-anchor check in 15 groups. These are checker flags at the first plan, not counts across retries or a semantic audit. It shows the guide's point that a new model trades one set of failures for another, so only a confirmation run tells you whether the trade holds.

cards.title: Why the smaller model won, and what the screen cannot say
questions: what explains the small model advantage in the guide
why did the 27b model beat the 32b in the local model guide
why did the smaller model win in the local model guide
is newer post-training the cause of the qwen3.8 result
what does the generation screen not separate
does the screen show why a smaller model outperformed the bigger one
what are the reasons a smaller model can outperform a bigger one on a task
can the screen prove a causal explanation for the qwen3.8 win
what is a configuration-level result
does a model that fits fully on the card run faster
what confounds were not separated in the generation screen
why can fit to the task beat parameter count
cards.answer: Newer post-training is one possible explanation, but the screen didn't separate it from architecture, quantisation, server, chat template or decoding differences, so it supports a configuration-level result, not a causal one. The guide gives general reasons a smaller model can win: a different or later training recipe can matter more than extra parameters, parameter count alone doesn't establish fit to a task's constraints, and quantisation, server and template change behavior. A model that fits fully on the card at the needed context also usually runs faster, which matters when a pipeline retries.

cards.title: Same model, different backend: the 3 versus 1 result
questions: what does the local model guide say about the same 32b accepting 3 groups and 1
how much does backend configuration change the same model's results
did qwen3-32b behave differently under different servers
does the serving stack change which groups a model passes
why must you compare configurations and not just models
how do quantisation server and template change model behaviour
how many groups did the same 32b accept under another backend configuration
what is the evidence that configuration matters in the guide
cards.answer: The guide cites it as evidence that a model name isn't the unit being tested: the same 32B accepted 3 groups under one backend configuration and 1 under another. Quantisation, server and chat template change behavior, so what I compared in the screen was configurations, one on Ollama and one on vLLM, not models in the abstract. That's why the method says to run the same model under each server and quantisation you're considering, with a control arm for each change, so you can attribute a difference to the thing you changed.

cards.title: What public benchmarks can and cannot tell you in the guide
questions: what can public benchmarks tell you according to the local model guide
how did gemma 4 score on ifeval in the generation screen
gemma 4 had the highest ifeval and accepted 0 of 20
why not use ifeval as the verdict for choosing a model
what are the ifeval scores 0.900 0.830 and 0.806
how did qwen3.8 rank on ifeval
what is benchmark contamination in the guide
how many task groups did gemma 4 exhaust plan and writing retries on
what does ifeval measure and not measure
should benchmark scores be used to build a shortlist
cards.answer: Use public benchmarks to build a shortlist, not as the verdict. In my screen, Gemma 4 had the highest IFEval score of the four models completed, 0.900 against the baseline's 0.830, and accepted 0 of 20 task groups: 3 exhausted their plan retries, 14 their writing retries, and the recorded refusal reasons show the other 3 stopped early after repeated failures. Qwen3.8 had the lowest, 0.806, and accepted the most. IFEval measures its own verifiable instructions, not every capability a pipeline needs, and public test material can leak into training data.

cards.title: Step one of the method: find candidates and check the licence
questions: how does the guide say to find candidate local models
what does step one of the model picking method say
why check the licence for an open-weight model
does open-weight mean unrestricted
what should I check about commercial and redistribution rights
what hardware constraints should shape a model shortlist
what reliability requirements should be written down alongside speed
why include the current model as the baseline
what obligations come with adapters or training data
how do you shortlist local models for a hardware budget
cards.answer: Start from what fits your hardware at the context, output length and concurrency you need, including the context cache and runtime overhead. Then shortlist from benchmarks, recent releases and the families you already run. Check each release's licence, acceptable-use terms and commercial and redistribution rights, plus any obligations that come with adapters or training data, because open-weight does not mean unrestricted. Write down reliability requirements alongside speed, including how failures, timeouts and exhausted retries will be handled, and include your current model as the baseline.

cards.title: Step two: turn the real task into a test
questions: does the guide count timeouts as failures
timeouts and failed answers in the denominator in the guide
how does the guide say to turn a real task into a test for local models
why keep failed and timed-out answers in the denominator
what should a frozen case set contain in the model selection method
how do you account for cost per successful case
should you test quality at long context length
what end to end accounting does the local model guide recommend
do advertised context limits prove quality at that length
why use code-based checks or answer keys when picking a model
what do you measure besides accuracy when choosing a local model
cards.answer: Freeze a set of real cases with code-based checks or answer keys, and keep failed and timed-out answers in the denominator so a model can't look better by failing quietly. Then account end to end: input and output tokens, retries, runtime and cost per successful case, plus latency and throughput. If you need long inputs, test quality at that length instead of trusting the advertised context limit. The idea is that the test measures your job, so the number you get is the one you'll live with in production.

cards.title: Writing the decision rule before the run
questions: how does the guide decide in advance what a win is
guide pre-registered decision rule before the run
what counts as a win in the model picking method
what does the guide say about writing the decision rule before you run
what should a pre-registered model comparison rule state
why must the lower bound of the interval clear the minimum useful improvement
what is the minimum useful improvement in the local model guide
why count groups not retries as independent units
how do you handle multiple candidates winning by luck
what multiplicity procedure does the guide suggest
does a rule written first remove small-sample uncertainty
what does a pass earn under a pre-registered rule
when do you stop testing under the guide's method
cards.answer: State the primary measure and the direction of comparison, the minimum useful improvement, the interval method and confidence level, how candidates are selected, when you'll stop, and what a pass earns. Require the interval's lower bound, not just the estimate, to clear the minimum useful improvement, and count groups or cases, not retries, as the independent units. A rule written first reduces discretion but doesn't remove small-sample uncertainty or the chance that one of several candidates wins by luck, so use a pre-specified multiplicity procedure or an independent confirmation design, finishing candidate selection before looking at confirmation results.

cards.title: Harness fidelity and checker validity
questions: does the guide validate the automatic checks before trusting results
validating checkers in the model selection method
what is harness fidelity in the local model guide
how do you reproduce the baseline within a stated tolerance
why does reproducing the baseline not prove the test is valid
how do you test the checks on known passing and failing examples
why review instructions for contradictions before evaluating models
should you audit a sample by hand or with a validated grader
what is checker validity in model evaluation
what does step four of the method say
how do you know your evaluation checks are correct
cards.answer: Reproduce the baseline within a stated tolerance and investigate any mismatch. Separately, test the checks on known passing, failing and borderline examples, review the instructions for contradictions, and audit a sample by hand or with a validated grader. Reproducing the baseline alone doesn't prove the test is valid, because a harness can reproduce an old number and still have a broken checker. The prompt conflict I found in my own screen is the example I'd point to: the pipeline ran faithfully, and the instruction set was still contradictory.

cards.title: Change one thing at a time and record everything
questions: how does the guide isolate variables
what goes in the run record in the model selection method
what to record for each model run in the guide
why change one thing at a time when choosing a local model
what settings does the guide say to record
should prompt changes be tested separately from model changes
does a shared seed guarantee identical runs
what do I need to record for reproducibility of a model comparison
which checkpoint and tokenizer details should be kept
why record the chat template and reasoning mode
what is a control arm for each change in the guide
how do you separate server quantisation prompt and model effects
cards.answer: Run the same model under each server and quantisation you're considering, and test prompt changes separately from model changes, so each difference has one cause. Record exact checkpoint and tokenizer revisions, chat template, server version, quantisation, reasoning mode, decoding settings, context and output budgets, stopping rules, retry policy and seeds. A shared seed doesn't guarantee identical runs, so I don't treat seeds as proof of reproducibility. The checklist asks the same thing: a control arm for each change and every setting recorded.

cards.title: Confirming a screening win on fresh cases
questions: does the guide rerun the winner on data it has not seen
how does the guide validate a model selection decision on fresh cases
confirmation round after a screening win in the guide
why confirm a screening win on fresh cases in the local model guide
what counts as fresh confirmation cases
what is a paired interval lower bound in the guide
can you prove what a vendor's model saw in training
what should be unused by local training prompt development or model selection
what does a screening win earn
why did the generation screen run a second round on 60 new groups
step six of the model picking method
how do you avoid overfitting a model choice to your dev set
cards.answer: A screening win earns a confirmation, not adoption. The confirmation uses cases not used in local training, prompt development or model selection, with a paired interval whose lower bound clears the minimum useful improvement. You can control what you used, but you usually can't prove what a vendor's model saw in training. My generation screen followed this: the 7 of 20 versus 3 screening result was followed by a second pre-registered round on 60 new groups, 24 accepted against 11, with a 95% interval of 6.6 to 35.5 on the difference.

cards.title: The order of levers before fine-tuning
questions: in what order does the guide say to try levers before fine-tuning
why does fine-tuning come last in the local model guide
what should you fix before fine-tuning a model
when is retrieval better than fine-tuning
when does the guide say to switch or route models
should you fix contradictions in instructions first
when is fine-tuning justified in the guide
what is the cheapest lever for improving a local model pipeline
can you use a different model per stage when failures differ by stage
cards.answer: The order is: fix the instructions and checks, switch or route models, add retrieval or tools, and only then fine-tune. Fixing instructions is low effort and always first, because contradictions between rules are common. Switching or routing needs evaluation time, and fits once a candidate meets your pre-registered rule and its confirmation; a different model per stage can help when failures differ by stage. Retrieval or tools fit when the problem is missing or changing knowledge, not behavior. Fine-tuning needs data, training and validation, so it's for when the best prompt and model still miss your bar and you can produce enough good, representative examples.

cards.title: Rejection-sampling fine-tuning and preference tuning
questions: what is rejection-sampling fine-tuning in the local model guide
how do automatic checks supply cheap labels for fine-tuning
what should you audit when fine-tuning on outputs that pass checks
what does the guide say about preference tuning and dpo
why can noisy preferences teach the wrong lesson
should preferences reflect quality rather than length or style
is a better first-try pass rate guaranteed after rejection sampling
what are the risks of reward-model based reinforcement learning in the guide
how do you build preference pairs for the same request
cards.answer: With rejection-sampling fine-tuning, automatic checks provide cheap labels for the properties they actually test. After validating the checks, you sample many outputs, keep those that pass and also meet your quality requirements, and fine-tune on them, auditing coverage, diversity and signs of the model exploiting the checks. A better first-try pass rate is a hypothesis to test on held-out cases, not a guarantee. Preference tuning pairs a preferred and a rejected response for the same request, and the preference has to reflect the quality you want, not length or style. Methods such as DPO or reward-model reinforcement learning can learn from the pairs, but noisy preferences teach the wrong lesson.

cards.title: LoRA and QLoRA on one GPU
questions: what do lora and qlora do in the local model guide
can a 27b model be fine-tuned on a 32 gb card
how does lora train small adapter weights
what is qlora over a frozen low-bit base
why must feasibility be measured for sequence length and batch size
what should be stored with a lora adapter
does lora freeze the base model
how many parameters does lora train
what are the single-gpu fine-tuning limits in the guide
cards.answer: LoRA trains small low-rank adapter weights while the base model usually stays frozen; how many weights that is depends on the rank and which layers are adapted. QLoRA does the same over a frozen low-bit copy of the base. That can make some 27B training runs feasible on a 32 GB card, but the guide is careful: feasibility must be measured for your sequence length, batch size and software. Keep the exact base checkpoint and the adapter's configuration together with the adapter, since the adapter is only meaningful against that base.

cards.title: How to validate a tuned model
questions: how does the guide check a tuned model did not regress on general skills
regression suite for a fine-tuned model in the guide
how does the guide say to validate a fine-tuned model
at what level should you split training and test sets
why de-duplicate at the level of related documents or templates
how do you compare tuned and untuned models like with like
what is a regression suite for a tuned model
how should the quality review of a tuned model be run
what should be reported besides the average for a tuned model
why keep the test set untouched until the decision point
what limits should be stated in advance for each guard
cards.answer: Split before you train, as whole cases, and de-duplicate at whatever level prevents leakage between related cases, documents or templates. Use validation data for tuning decisions and keep the test set untouched until the decision point. Run tuned and untuned models on the same base checkpoint, server, quantisation, prompt and settings, and record any differences you can't remove. Guard what the checks can't see with a small regression suite and a pre-specified quality review, with a rubric, stated sample size and sampling procedure, blinded where feasible, with limits stated in advance and subgroup and stage-level failures reported, not just the average.

cards.title: Null results, release and the fine-tuning experiment status
questions: what does the guide say if my fine-tune does not beat the base model
fine-tune null result in the local model guide
how should a null result from fine-tuning be interpreted in the guide
does a failed fine-tuning test show fine-tuning cannot help
what is the status of the fine-tuning experiment from the local model guide
when will the fine-tuning results be added to the guide
how does a tuned model that passes get released
what limits does the local model guide have
what does the guide say about a small live trial and a way back
is the fine-tuning part of the guide finished
does the guide cover results of tuning the generation screen model
cards.answer: A failed test of one recipe doesn't show that fine-tuning cannot help; it shows that this data, recipe and setup did not clear the bar. A tuned model that does pass still goes through the normal release route: a small live trial, a quality review and a way back. As for status, a fine-tuning experiment following this method is designed for the generation screen, and its results will be added when it finishes. So the guide's fine-tuning sections are method, not reported results, and run results are specific to the configurations and cases tested.

cards.title: The one-page model selection checklist
questions: what does the guide check before adopting an open-weight model
one page checklist for picking an open-weight model
what is on the one-page checklist in the local model guide
what questions does the model selection checklist ask
what is a good answer to did I decide what better means first
does the checklist ask about licence and acceptable use
what does the checklist say about fit at context and concurrency
what does the checklist require before fine-tuning
what does the checklist say about keeping the test set apart
what does the checklist say the winner must show on fresh cases
give me the model picking checklist
cards.answer: It's ten questions, each with a good answer. Does the model fit at my context, output length and concurrency, measured on my hardware including cache? Is the licence checked for the exact release? Is the test my real task with validated checks? Did I fix what better means first, in a written rule frozen before the run? Does the current model reproduce its known result? Are server, quantisation, prompt and model separated? Did the winner hold on fresh cases? Did I fix instructions and try other models before fine-tuning? Is the test set kept apart? Did general skill and quality hold within limits stated in advance?
